slides.title: Unit economics
At the median of Parcelbird's own customer sites, each order would lose $6.17, and riders are the largest drain

claims.claim: At the median of Parcelbird's own customer sites, each order would lose $6.17
evidence: Per order, 14 customer sites, 2025: Margin on goods 9.18; Delivery fee 1.99; Promotions -2.04; Picking and packing -3.1; Payment and packaging -1.3; Riders -7.3958; Store fixed cost -3.5008
Margin on goods = 27% of a $34 basket; promotions 6% of it; riders = $17.75 an hour ÷ 2.4 orders; store fixed cost = $1.15M a year ÷ 900 orders a day, all year

claims.claim: Rider cost, not rent, sinks the median order
evidence: 80.6% of the margin on each order's goods goes to the rider
Riders: at 2.4 orders an hour, rider time is the cost that density must cut

claims.claim: Before store costs: the order still loses $2.67, so filling the store alone does not fix it
Break-even: the median basket would have to grow to about $63, 1.9 times today's
Our software is in the data: these 14 sites already run on Parcelbird's software

slides.title: A site matching the best on every driver would still lose about $1.80 an order; the founders' plan assumes more

claims.claim: A site matching the best on every driver would still lose about $1.80 an order
evidence: Contribution per order after store costs: Columbus pop-up −$12.6; Benchmark median −$6.2; Best observed −$1.8; Founders' plan $2.02
Best basket and best density come from different sites; no site achieved both

claims.claim: Only the plan turns positive and it needs every driver above any site on record
evidence: Average order value: pop-up $31; median $34; best $42; plan $45 — Plan above the best site
Orders per rider-hour: 2.1; 2.4; 3; 3.5 — Plan above the top of the range
Orders per site per day: 280; 900; 1,400; 1,800 — Plan above the top of the range
Promotions, % of basket: 12%; 6%; 6%; 2% — Plan at a third of the median
Benchmark ranges: 1.9–3.0 orders per rider-hour, 400–1,400 orders per site per day
Pop-up result uses its own annualised fixed cost of $0.65M

slides.title: Resetting either basket size or rider speed alone to the median turns the plan's profit into a loss

claims.claim: Resetting either basket size or rider speed alone to the median turns the plan's profit into a loss
evidence: Plan contribution per order: Founders' plan as modelled 2.0182; Basket size at the median -0.7318; Rider speed at the median -0.3062; Store volume at the median 0.2678; Promotions at the median 0.2182
Each bar changes one driver of the founders' plan to the benchmark median and keeps the others at plan values

claims.claim: Two of the four drivers each carry the whole profit
evidence: Basket size: the plan's $45 is 32% above the median, and no site has reached it
Rider speed: the plan needs riders 46% faster than the median, above any site's pace

claims.claim: Volume and promotions: either one alone leaves the plan barely above zero
Both at the median: the plan would lose about $3.06 an order, half the median site's loss

slides.title: Copying Zipcart's fix is not enough: a median site with its fee and promotion cut would still lose $1.05 an order

claims.claim: a median site with its fee and promotion cut would still lose $1.05 an order
evidence: −$6.2 at the benchmark median today
+ $3.99 new service fee on every order, as Zipcart charged
+ $1.7 saved by cutting promotions from 6% to 1% of a $34 basket
− $0.6 more store cost per order once volume falls 14%, as in Zipcart's city
= −$1.05 per order at a median site with Zipcart's fixes
Riders keep the median pace of 2.4 orders an hour, and the fee is kept in full
Volume falls 14% after the fee: 900 orders a day become about 774

claims.claim: Zipcart's result needed top-of-range density, which the pop-up was far from
evidence: Break-even with these fixes needs about 1,042 orders a day, 16% above the median and 3.7 times the pop-up's 280
At the best site's 1,400 orders a day, the same fixes would earn about $0.41, close to Zipcart's $0.40

slides.title: Four gates tell the board when to reopen quick commerce, starting with proof from customer sites

claims.claim: Four gates tell the board when to reopen quick commerce
evidence: 1 Site economics: Orders a day a customer site holds with a $3.99 fee and 1% promotions; threshold 1,042; Quarterly, from customer-site data; Reopen with a one-store test sized inside the headroom
2 Runway: Cash against 12 months of burn; threshold $4.8M; Monthly; Hold hires and cut discretionary spend
3 Software pipeline: New ARR signed by end of 2027, at least the hires' cost; threshold $0.8M; Mid-2027 and year end; If under half by mid-2027, hold the second pair of hires
4 Rider pay rules: Minimum pay standards for delivery workers; Any adoption; each $1 an hour adds $0.42 an order; As each city decides; Re-run the break-even before any reopening
Gate 1 is the break-even volume with Zipcart's fee and promotion cut at median rider speed; gate 2 is 12 months × today's $0.4M burn

claims.claim: Until the first gate is met, fast grocery delivery stays a software opportunity for Parcelbird, not an operating one
